leads.name: The Golden Rain Tree of Aldenhofpark
leads.access: Free, Aldenhofpark is an open public park, gemeente-owned, visitable at any time
leads.story:
It flowers in July, which is the point of it. Almost every tree in a Dutch park has finished flowering by midsummer; the golden rain tree waits, then covers itself in loose yellow panicles for weeks. What follows is stranger. The spent flowers become papery three-sided lanterns, pink turning to brown, hollow with a seed rattling inside, and they hang on well past the point where the leaves have gone orange and dropped.

The Dutch call it the lampionboom, the lantern tree, and it comes from China and Korea. That is roughly why it is here: the national register of monumental trees lists it on dendrological grounds, which is the designation given to a tree that earns protection for what it is rather than for anything it has witnessed.

It is also, honestly, the whole of what is known. The register puts it at about a century old and records no history for it, no girth and no height, and we found no walking route, article or archive that names a golden rain tree in Aldenhofpark. So this one is a register entry with a real tree at the end of it, standing in the north section of the park on city ground that is open at any hour. If you know its story, we would like to hear it.

best_time.label: July and August, when it flowers yellow and nothing around it does

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by loose yellow flower clusters in July, followed by papery three-sided seed pods that hang on after the leaves have gone. It stands in the north section of Aldenhofpark.
leads.removed_reason: Dead or felled per the register itself: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1691693 carries status 5, Dood/geveld (checked 2026-10-10 against the Bomenstichting ArcGIS layer). Inspector remark: "Oude lampionboom die op 28 augustus 1987 tot Rosseelsboom is gedoopt. Aan de stamvoet wordt al enige tijd de dikrandtonderzwam aangetroffen (12-3-2003). In 2021 als geveld aangeduid." Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry.

leads.name: The Sweet Gum of Waldeckpark

location.address: Waldeckpark, near the roundabout, western section, Maastricht

leads.access: Free, Waldeckpark is an open public park, gemeente-owned, visitable at any time
leads.story:
Its Latin name means liquid amber, and it earned it: cut the bark of a sweet gum and it bleeds a fragrant resin that North Americans chewed like gum and burned like incense. The leaf looks like a maple's, five points and a long stalk, and the tree is not remotely a maple. It is a cousin of witch hazel, and it holds its colour later into the year than almost anything else standing in Waldeckpark.

When it was planted is a question the paperwork itself hedges. The national register of monumental trees notes that it was most likely put in when Leonard Springer laid out this park in 1921, and most likely is the register's own wording rather than ours. Springer's design is documented: a romantic layout on the demolished Waldeck bastion, with a rose avenue and the old fortification ruins left in place. Whether this particular tree belongs to that planting is not recorded anywhere we could reach, so call it roughly a hundred years old and leave the rest open.

No girth or height has been published for it either. It stands near the roundabout at the western end of the park, on city ground, free and open. Somebody with a tape measure could improve this entry in ten minutes.

best_time.label: late October into November, when one tree carries red, orange and purple at once

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its maple-like five-pointed leaf and, if you scratch the bark, a fragrant resin. It stands near the roundabout at the western end of Waldeckpark.
leads.removed_reason: Dead or felled per the register itself: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1691694 carries status 5, Dood/geveld (checked 2026-10-10 against the Bomenstichting ArcGIS layer). Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry.

leads.name: The Japanese Maple of Waldeckpark
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB v2024), Bomenstichting, register nr 1678456: 'Japanse esdoorn', Waldeckpark, planted band 1910-1920, owner_category gemeente, setting park, visitable ja

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldeckpark (confirms Waldeckpark was laid out in 1921 by Leonard Springer on the former Bastion Waldeck, is a public municipal park with monumental trees, though does not name this specific specimen)
leads.access: Free. Stands in Waldeckpark on Prins Bisschopsingel, a municipally owned public park; open at all times like any city park.
leads.transport: Short walk from Maastricht city centre and from the other Waldeckpark/Aldenhofpark trees already published (maa_012, maa_013, maa_014); the busy Prins Bisschopsingel road separates it from the adjoining Stadspark, so cross at the signalled crossing.
leads.story:
The national register puts this Japanese maple in the planting years 1910 to 1920. The park around it was laid out in 1921. Both statements come from good sources and nobody has reconciled them: either the maple was already standing on the old Bastion Waldeck before Leonard Springer drew his park over the demolished fortification, or the register's decade band is simply loose. Worth knowing, and not yet written down anywhere.

What the band does give is a bracket of roughly 106 to 116 years, which is a long life for Acer palmatum. The species is a slow, small tree, planted across Europe since the nineteenth century as a garden ornament and rarely allowed to get old; most of the Japanese maples anyone has met are shrubs you can see over the top of. This one has had a century in municipal ground, which is why the register marks it as dendrologically notable rather than merely present.

It is also, so far, a tree only one source names. Waldeckpark and the Stadspark it adjoins hold more than 800 trees between them across some 160 species, and the histories of the park describe that collection without singling this specimen out. It stands with the park's Caucasian wingnut, golden rain tree and sweet gum, four trees in a few minutes of walking.
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small palm-shaped leaves, cut into five to seven narrow lobes and scarlet in October, on a low tree rather than one of the park's tall ones. It stands in Waldeckpark, off Prins Bisschopsingel.

best_time.label: October and November, when the leaves run from orange into deep red

leads.removed_reason: Dead or felled per the register itself: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1678456 carries status 5, Dood/geveld (checked 2026-10-10 against the Bomenstichting ArcGIS layer). Inspector remark: "Aangelegd door L.Springer in 1921. Schitterende herfstkleur! De esdoorn is niet meer aanwezig (12-3-2003)." Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry.

blocked.name: Osagedoorn (Stadspark, Maasboulevard)
blocked.reason: LIKELY DEAD / NOT THE REGISTERED TREE: the LRMB register lists this Osage orange at Stadspark/Maasboulevard with a planted_band of 1880-1890, but IVN Maastricht's own Stadspark tree-walk page (https://www.ivn.nl/afdeling/maastricht/bomenwandeling-van-hemel-tot-fossiel/) states the park's Osage orange (Maclura pomifera/Goudappel) was 130 years old when it fell in October 2009, and was replaced with a new planting in 2011. If this register point is that same spot, the tree standing there today is a c.15-year-old replacement, not the historic specimen the register's date describes, and it is not yet a remarkable/collectible tree. The register carries no vitality field and was not updated to reflect the loss. Needs an on-the-ground or dated-aerial-imagery check before ever being considered again: confirm whether the current tree is the young 2011 replacement (block stands) or whether this register point is actually a different, still-living Osage orange elsewhere in the park (in which case re-open). RE-CHECKED 2026-09-09: no new evidence found this pass; not re-litigated, block stands per brief instruction.

blocked.name: Treurginkgo (Polvertorenplein)
blocked.reason: PRIVATE PROPERTY: the register itself places this tree 'in particuliere tuin van een nieuwbouwwoning' (in the private garden of a newly built house, since 2021), with owner_category particulier, visitable 'onbekend' and visible only 'beperkt' (limited). Fails hard rule 10's no-permission-needed test outright: this is somebody's home. A genuinely interesting specimen (reportedly brought from Japan around 1800 by G.J. Colpin) but not publishable under any circumstance while it stands in a private residential garden.

blocked.name: Gewone plataan (Sint Lambertuslaan 6, Villa Marguerite)
blocked.reason: The register marks this 'visitable: ja', but Villa Marguerite is a private 1890 villa (national monument for its architecture, per rijksmonumenten.nl) in Maastricht's residential 'Villapark', currently divided into rentable apartments. No evidence of any public path, garden opening, or business use that would let a stranger walk up to this tree without knocking on a resident's door. The register's 'visitable' field appears to describe whether the tree itself is inspectable in principle, not whether the public may enter the grounds. Fails hard rule 10's no-permission-needed test; blocked as a private garden unless future evidence shows the grounds are genuinely open (e.g. a public event, a through-path, or commercial/institutional use of the building).
